title: Aperture Labs — POC scoping (latency SLOs & benchmarks)
summary: POC scoping call to align on latency and throughput SLOs for Aperture's realtime assistant use case. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT definitions, p95/p99 targets for short and long prompts, measurement plan (synthetic vs production replay), workload sizing, and timeline. Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide benchmark harness, run an initial 2-week benchmark (1 week setup + 1 week runs) across three model variants, Aperture to share representative traces and evaluation prompts, and schedule follow-up with infra and security stakeholders.
topics: Define TTFT and TPOT for Aperture's assistant
Set p95/p99 SLO targets for short/long prompts
Measurement plan: client vs server timing, synthetic vs replay benchmarks
Workload sizing: qps, batch sizes, sequence lengths
Tradeoffs: dedicated vs hosted, batching, quantization, KV/prefix cache
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark harness + instructions (link to private repo) by 2027-12-16
Aperture to export 48 hours of representative production traces and 200 evaluation prompts by 2027-12-18
Run initial benchmark across 3 model variants (open base, quantized, redwood-optimized) during week of 2027-12-20
Follow-up meeting to review results and SLO recommendations on 2028-01-04
action_items: Samir: Share benchmark harness repo and example infra templates (due 2027-12-16)
Maya: Provide prod traces, traffic profiles, and success criteria doc (due 2027-12-18)
Jess: Prepare a recommended benchmark config (models, batch sizes, synthetic vs replay) and run initial smoke test (due 2027-12-19)
Nora: Confirm security contacts for Private/Dedicated discussions (due 2027-12-20)
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samir from Redwood here. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Maya: Maya Singh, Head of Platform at Aperture. Hey Samir, hi Jess.
[00:11] Eric: Eric Liao, ML Eng.
[00:13] Nora: Nora Park, SRE.
[00:15] Samir: Great. Goal today is to scope the PoC for latency/throughput SLOs — TTFT vs TPOT — and agree a measurement plan. Roughly 45–60 minutes. Sound good?
[00:25] Maya: Yep. We want clear p95/p99 targets and a runnable bench we can reproduce.
[00:29] Jess: Awesome. Real quick, can you describe the workload? QPS, typical prompt lengths, streaming or single-response?
[00:36] Eric: Primary is realtime assistant for customers on live calls — short prompts, usually 5–30 tokens, sometimes follow-ups that extend the sequence to ~400 tokens. Peak qps ~120, steady ~30. We use streaming for user-facing UI.
[00:50] Samir: Perfect, that shapes the SLOs — short-turn TTFT is critical for UX, and TPOT matters for long responses and cost. Just to align our terms: we use TTFT = time-to-first-token (client receives first model token), TPOT = time-per-token from server-side generation. Is that consistent?
[01:10] Eric: Yes that's what we care about. Also cold-starts are painful for interactive sessions.
[01:15] Jess: Noted. For measurement, we'll capture both client-side observed TTFT and server-side metrics — so we can separate network and scheduling from model inference. We'll instrument both.
[01:26] Nora: How do you separate network latency from TTFT? Our SREs will want server-only numbers to validate infra.
[01:31] Samir: Good call. Plan is: client ping to get request start timestamp, server records accept time and first-token emit time. TTFT_client = first_token_received - client_request_sent; TTFT_server = first_token_sent - server_request_received. Then we have TPOT_server = (time_of_token_n - time_of_token_n-1) averaged for the stream window.
[01:50] Maya: We need p95/p99 targets, can you propose realistic numbers?
[01:54] Jess: Based on similar customers: for short prompts (<=30 tokens) on dedicated GPU pools we typically target TTFT_server p95 < 120–200ms, p99 < 350–450ms. TTFT_client will add network, so p95 ~200–300ms depending on region. TPOT_server for steady token emission: p95 < 20–40ms/token, p99 < 60–100ms/token depending on model size and quantization.
[02:20] Eric: That's helpful. For our UX team, if TTFT_client p95 < 250ms and p99 < 500ms we're happy. For longer completions (400 tokens) total generation time should feel <8s p95 ideally.
[02:33] Samir: Ok, translate that: 400 tokens * 20ms/token = 8s at p95 if TPOT 20ms. So we need both low TTFT and low TPOT. We should set tiered SLOs: short-turn SLOs and long-turn SLOs.
[02:46] Jess: Agreed. Proposed SLOs (draft): Short-turn (<=30 tokens): TTFT_server p95 < 150ms, p99 < 400ms; TTFT_client p95 < 300ms, p99 < 600ms. Long-turn (>200 tokens): TPOT_server p95 < 30ms/token, p99 < 80ms/token, and total gen p95 < 9s.
[03:03] Maya: That looks reasonable. Are those achievable on hosted or do we need Dedicated?
[03:08] Samir: Depends on model and traffic. Hosted can hit those for moderate qps with optimized models; for peak sustained qps and isolation, Dedicated is safer. Also KV/prefix caching will reduce TTFT on repeated prompts.
[03:20] Nora: Can caching help cold starts? We still see slow cold JVMs and model load times when we scale up nodes.
[03:27] Jess: Cold start for a GPU-backed container is primarily model load time and kernel JIT. In Redwood Dedicated we can keep warm pools to avoid cold starts. For the bench we should measure both cold and warm start p95/p99 explicitly.
[03:40] Ben Ortiz: (brief) Also want cost estimates — if we hit these SLOs what are the obvious cost drivers?
[03:45] Samir: Main levers: model size (bigger = more GPU time), batching (improves throughput but can add latency tail), quantization (lowers cost with small latency tradeoffs), and reserved capacity vs burst. We'll include cost estimates per model profile in the bench report.
[03:58] Eric: On batching — our traffic is spiky. How does Continuous batching affect TTFT?
[04:03] Jess: Continuous batching groups requests with short time windows. For latency-sensitive traffic you configure max wait time (e.g., 5–15ms) and prefer small batches. We'll test several batching configs: no batching, 4–8 request batches, and larger batch for throughput scenarios.
[04:17] Maya: Measurement plan detail? We need reproducible runs and to understand synthetic vs production replay.
[04:22] Samir: Two-pronged: 1) Synthetic benchmarks with controlled qps, seq len, batch configs — good for apples-to-apples model comparisons. 2) Production replay using trace data — inject real request patterns into the bench harness to see realistic tail effects. We'll run both.
[04:36] Nora: For replay, we'll scrub PII and replace user content — will Redwood accept traces as anonymized logs?
[04:42] Samir: Yes, anonymized traces are fine. We'll provide a script to scrub identifiers.
[04:46] Jess: Also we'll capture server metrics (accept time, first_token_sent, token timestamps), container metrics (GPU utilization, mem), and Redwood Console traces for per-route breakdown. We'll produce p50/p95/p99 for TTFT_server, TTFT_client, TPOT, plus cost per 1k tokens.
[05:01] Eric: For TPOT, do you measure inter-token intervals server-side only?
[05:05] Jess: Correct. We'll log token timestamps and compute median inter-token time and p95/p99. For streaming we also measure end-to-end perceived throughput to clients.
[05:13] Maya: What model variants will you test?
[05:16] Samir: We suggest three variants: 1) Open base (non-quantized), 2) Quantized (int8) version, 3) Redwood-optimized/compiled variant with kernel optimizations. We'll include a smaller model if you want ultra-low TTFT.
[05:32] Eric: Yes include a small low-latency model as a baseline.
[05:35] Jess: Great. We'll also test with KV/prefix cache for repeated prompts; measure cache hit effect on TTFT.
[05:43] Nora: How long do the runs take? If we're testing multiple configs and traces, we could easily be 1–2 weeks.
[05:49] Samir: Proposed PoC timeline: 1 week for setup (repo, traces, infra templates), 1 week of benchmark runs (multiple configs + replay), 1 week for analysis and recommendations — total 3 weeks. If you want a quicker iteration, we can scope a 2-week pilot: 3 days setup, 4 days runs, 3 days analysis.
[06:07] Maya: Let's do the full 3-week cycle. Need that analysis for QBR.
[06:11] Ben: Security/compliance — we'll need SOC2 and network diagrams before Dedicated conversation.
[06:16] Samir: We'll share SOC2 report and architecture docs. For Private deployments, we can provide VPC architecture and KMS integrations.
[06:23] Nora: Also RBAC and audit logs — we need per-request audit traces for compliance.
[06:28] Jess: Redwood Console has request-level traces and token-level cost breakdowns; we'll enable audit log export to your SIEM in the PoC.
[06:35] Eric: On measurement tooling — what does the harness look like? Is it a client we run in our cloud?
[06:40] Samir: We'll provide a containerized harness you can run in your environment or our test infra. It supports synthetic generators and replay mode (ingests trace files). It outputs CSVs and a dashboard. We'll include examples and infra-as-code to spin up test workers.
[06:54] Maya: We'll need instructions for running in our VPC.
[06:57] Samir: We'll include Terraform snippets and IAM perms required.
[07:02] Jess: Let's talk measurement specifics: buckets and sample sizes. For p99 stability we need tens of thousands of requests per config; for replay the natural traffic should provide that, otherwise we'll amplify. We'll run each config for at least 30m steady-state plus a few spike windows.
[07:18] Nora: Amplification — careful about cost and rate limits.
[07:21] Samir: We'll work with aperture to request temporary higher quota if needed.
[07:25] Eric: Any automated alerts or SLO monitoring integration?
[07:28] Jess: We'll suggest SLO alerts hooked into your PagerDuty for p99 regressions and Redwood Console can emit SLO status metrics to Prometheus.
[07:36] Maya: For the p95/p99 numbers you proposed earlier, can you put those in the bench config so the run fails if SLOs aren't met?
[07:43] Samir: Yes, we can add SLO assertions into the harness. We'll also produce a final report with violations highlighted.
[07:49] Ben: Cost modeling — please include cost per 1M tokens and cost delta between quantized and non-quantized.
[07:55] Samir: Will do. We'll include a cost sensitivity table.
[07:59] Eric: A couple of nitty-gritty items: how do you account for client-side jitter in p95 client numbers?
[08:04] Jess: We'll gather client-side metrics from synthetic runners placed in your regions to simulate typical network conditions. We'll also provide separate network-only baseline measurements with an echo endpoint.
[08:15] Maya: For the replay, we have several endpoints — web, mobile, and an SDK. Should we test all three?
[08:21] Samir: Recommend starting with web and SDK (these are highest qps). If those pass, expand to mobile.
[08:27] Nora: One more ops ask: if we need Dedicated, what are the autoscale knobs?
[08:31] Samir: Autoscaling policies can scale by queue depth, GPU utilization, or latency. For strict SLOs we typically combine a min warm pool + reactive autoscale. We'll include example policies.
[08:45] Eric: Cool. Any gotchas with model compilation/JIT causing p99 spikes mid-run?
[08:50] Jess: Yes, JIT warm-up can create spikes. We'll run warm-up phases before measuring and include cold-start experiments separately. Also kernel selection might change if sequence length distribution shifts, so we test variable seq lengths.
[09:03] Maya: Okay, let's recap to make sure we're aligned.
[09:05] Samir: Recap: Redwood provides harness and infra templates; Aperture shares anonymized traces and prompts; run 3-model variant bench with synthetic and replay modes; capture TTFT_server, TTFT_client, TPOT p50/p95/p99, GPU metrics, cost; run warm/cold experiments; produce report, cost table and SLO recommendations. Timeline: start setup immediately, full PoC 3 weeks, follow-up 2028-01-04.
[09:28] Maya: That matches our expectations.
[09:30] Ben: Thx — we'll loop in security after you share docs.
[09:33] Samir: I'll send the repo link and instructions after the call. Link: (repo private link) — also sharing benchmark spreadsheet (sheet link) with config matrix.
[09:40] Eric: One last detail — do you have example thresholds for p99 perturbations that count as regression?
[09:45] Jess: Typical rule: >20% increase in p99 over baseline triggers an investigation, >50% triggers rollback/fallback policy. We can tune those thresholds.
[09:54] Nora: Make sure audit logs are enabled for the reroutes.
[09:57] Samir: Noted. Anything else?
[09:59] Maya: No, thanks everyone.
[10:02] Samir: Great, we'll follow up with the harness and schedule. Appreciate your time.
[10:06] (call ends)
